problems.stem: An AI email draft to your professor names her 'Dr. Smith' but your professor is Dr. Lee, and it invents office hours. What is the right move before sending?
options: Send it; the AI usually gets names right
Read and verify the recipient name, dates, and any claimed facts, then fix them
Add more exclamation points so it sounds friendly
problems.explanation: AI does not know your real professor or schedule. Always check names, dates, and facts before the email leaves your outbox.

problems.stem: You want to ask for a two-day extension. Which prompt gives the AI enough to draft a usable email?
options: Write an email to my professor
Write a short, polite email to Prof. Lee for CAT 100 requesting a 2-day extension on the Module 7 lab, due Friday, because I was ill
problems.explanation: The specific prompt names the recipient, course, exact request, deadline, and reason. A one-line prompt yields a generic draft you cannot use.

problems.stem: Which opening best fits an email to a professor about a grade question?
options: Hey can u bump my grade thx
Subject: CAT 100 Lab 3 grade question -- Dear Dr. Lee, I have a question about the rubric points on Lab 3
yo prof whats up with this grade
TO WHOM IT MAY CONCERN: I DEMAND A REVIEW
problems.explanation: A professor audience needs a clear subject line, a named greeting, and a specific, calm request. Casual or aggressive tone undercuts the ask.

problems.stem: You ask a public AI tool to draft an email about a missed exam. What should you keep out of the prompt?
options: The fact that you missed an exam
Your full student ID number and a private medical note; use a placeholder like [STUDENT ID] instead
problems.explanation: Sensitive identifiers and medical details should not go into a public tool. Draft with a placeholder, then fill the private value in yourself.
